newsitem.title: FRANCE: Gelatine producers deny BSE cover-up.
newsitem.headline: Gelatine producers deny BSE cover-up.

text.p: European gelatine manufacturers denied on Thursday they had witheld important information from the European Commission on the public health risk of gelatine manufacturing methods.

"There has never been any attempt to bring influence to bear on the work of any bodies," Reinhard Schrieber, the head of the Gelatine Manufacturers of Europe (GME), told the European Parliament's committee of inquiry into mad cow disease (BSE).
The European Commission on June 11 approved new processing techniques, thought to make gelatine safe from the agent which causes BSE, on the basis of a 1994 report from the GME.
On June 14 the Commission was sent a new report from the GME saying more research was needed before the processing techniques could be declared safe.
Lars Hoelgaard, a senior veterinary official in the Commission, slammed the GME on Tuesday for not submitting the the second report, finalised on April 9, at an earlier date.
But Schreiber said the Commission had refused to meet the gelatine manufacturers earlier.
"We had asked to be able to present our case. That had been turned down," he insisted. "Then the Commission said, 'We want the facts.' We made the facts available the very same day."

In April, the GME sent the final report to a German member of the European Union scientific veterinary committee on whose recommendation the Commission approved the new techniques. They had also told the German Health Ministry.
Schrieber said the GME had assumed the scientist, Professor Ring, would inform the rest of the EU scientific committee.
"As far as I'm concerned, passing over a document to a German member of the committee is commensurate to passing information to the committee itself," he said.
Schrieber said the manufacturers had never asked for an end to the ban on making gelatine from raw materials from Britain or any other country where a BSE epidemic develops.
"We know we couldn't market the product because consumers wouldn't buy it," he explained.
He said the argument about the ban and whether any processing technique could render raw materials from infected cattle safe had done immense damage to the industry.
"I think the whole affair...was extremely detrimental as far as the industry was concerned," he said.
